eligibility_reason: ReMe distills execution trajectories into structured experiences (success patterns, failure lessons, comparative insights) at run time and stores them in an experience pool (vector database) that is queried on later, new tasks to condition the agent's future behaviour (p. 1 abstract; p. 4, Section 3.2-3.3; p. 13, Appendix). The store is written by the agent's own pipeline, not a fixed corpus (E3 does not apply), memory is externalised rather than parametric (E2 does not apply), this is a primary study proposing a novel framework rather than a survey (E4 does not apply), and the paper is 21 pages with substantial empirical evaluation (E7 does not apply). Year given as 2025, English, full text available.

facets.justification: p. 4, Section 3.2: 'All retained experiences are indexed by the embedding vector of usage scenario ω and then stored in a vector database, which we refer to as the experience pool.' p. 13, Appendix: 'Our selected vector database is Elasticsearch.' The framework diagram (Fig. 2, p. 4) shows acquisition, reuse and refinement all operating on this single indexed pool, so this is not a deliberately combined multi_store contribution.

p. 1 abstract and p. 4, Section 3.2: the 'multi-faceted distillation' mechanism (LLMsumm) performs 'comparative analysis by jointly examining successful and failed trajectories, identifying critical differences that distinguish effective from ineffective attempts' — content generated by comparing multiple trajectories, not present in any single source item, matching reflect_synthesize. The framework also prunes low-utility entries ('utility-based deletion', Fig. 2, p. 4), an edit_in_place-like operation, but distillation is named first in the contribution list (p. 2) and is the mechanism whose capability is ablated as the primary driver of gains (Table 5, p. 8), so it is coded as the primary write transformation.

p. 4, Section 3.3: top-K experiences are retrieved by cosine similarity over embeddings of the task query ('computes cosine similarity scores to rank prior experiences'), then 'we optionally employ a context-aware reranker LLMrerank to further refine the selection.' The abstract (p. 1/2) and intro (p. 2) declare this as one pipeline: 'usage scenario indexing strategy for retrieval, supplemented by reranking and adaptive rewriting.' The reranking prompt (Table 14, p. 19) is a declared second, LLM-judged ranking signal layered on the similarity_topk retrieval, matching the guide's re-ranking-rule criterion for hybrid.

Evaluated on BFCL-V3 and AppWorld benchmarks with baseline comparisons and ablations across model scales (Qwen3-8B/14B/32B) and retrieval-key variants (p. 8, Table 5, Fig. 4-5; p. 13, Table 8-9). No deployed system, real users, or field setting is reported anywhere in the extracted pages — conservative validation coding per the guide.

Results are reported as scores (Avg@4, Pass@4) over fixed benchmark suites BFCL-V3 and AppWorld against a No-Memory baseline and across backbones (p. 8, Table 5-6; p. 13, Table 8-9), the defining pattern of benchmark_evaluation.

p. 1 abstract and p. 2 contribution list: 'we propose ReMe ..., a comprehensive framework for experience-driven agent evolution' that 'integrates multi-faceted experience distillation, context-adaptive reuse, and utility-based refinement.' The paper argues for an integrated, multi-mechanism architecture over the memory lifecycle (Fig. 2, p. 4) rather than a single technique; code and a dataset are released but are secondary to the architecture per the contribution list (p. 2).
